Name: Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value
Description: The product does not validate or incorrectly validates the integrity check values or "checksums" of a message.

ModesOfIntroduction.Note: REALIZATION: This weakness is caused during implementation of an architectural security tactic.

CommonConsequences.Note: Integrity checks usually use a secret key that helps authenticate the data origin. Skipping integrity checking generally opens up the possibility that new data from an invalid source can be injected.
Data that is parsed and used may be corrupted.
Without a checksum check, it is impossible to determine if any changes have been made to the data after it was sent.

DetectionMethods.Description: Automated static analysis, commonly referred to as Static Application Security Testing (SAST), can find some instances of this weakness by analyzing source code (or binary/compiled code) without having to execute it. Typically, this is done by building a model of data flow and control flow, then searching for potentially-vulnerable patterns that connect "sources" (origins of input) with "sinks" (destinations where the data interacts with external components, a lower layer such as the OS, etc.)

PotentialMitigations.Description: The protocol specification describes the algorithm used for calculating the checksum. It is then a matter of implementing the calculation and verifying that the calculated checksum and the received checksum match.

Entries.IntroText: The following example demonstrates the weakness.

ObservedExamples.Description: network analysis tool does not properly validate an integrity check value, allowing installation of malicious firmware
